title: Fourth and Walnut (1958)
hookLine: on a Louisville street corner he suddenly loves everyone he sees

lines: A MARKER ON A STREET CORNER.
cards: Louisville, Kentucky, March 18, 1958. A monk from Gethsemani is in town on an errand, standing at a busy corner in the shopping district, Fourth and Walnut, waiting to cross. Shoppers, office workers, people in a hurry.
Nothing special. And then, in the middle of that ordinary crowd, something happens to him that he'll write about for the rest of his life. Today a historical marker stands on that corner.

teach.b: First, the moment. Merton tells it in his book Conjectures of a Guilty Bystander. Standing on that corner, he was suddenly overwhelmed by the realization that he loved all these people.
They were his, and he was theirs. Total strangers, and yet not strangers at all. Second, the waking.

teach.h: WAKING FROM A DREAM OF SEPARATENESS.
teach.b: He describes it as waking from a dream: the dream that monks are separate, special, holier than the people out on the street. He'd spent years behind a wall, and all at once the wall felt like an illusion.
He was one of them, a human being among human beings, and glad of it. Third, the shining.

teach.h: THEY WERE ALL SHINING LIKE THE SUN.
teach.b: He wrote that he wished he could tell people they were all shining like the sun.
Not because they were perfect, but because of who they were before God, underneath everything: what he called the point in each person that belongs to God alone, untouched by sin or illusion.

The Gospels have that picture too. At the Transfiguration, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus's "face did shine as the sun." And in Matthew, Jesus says that one day "the just shine as the sun, in the kingdom of their Father."
Merton saw a glimpse of it on a street corner. Fourth, why it matters. Some readers see this as a turning point in his life as a monk.
Afterward, he wrote more and more about the world outside: race, war, and the people on the street.

teach.h: THE JUST SHINE AS THE SUN.
teach.b: Contemplation hadn't taken him away from people. It had sent him back to them.

how: Visitors to Louisville can see the historical marker for Merton's experience at Fourth and Walnut, now Fourth and Muhammad Ali Boulevard, and some Catholic retreats use the passage to talk about seeing Christ in strangers.

games.why: Merton wrote that he suddenly loved them all, and that the idea of being separate from them was a dream he'd woken from.

practice: If there are people around you, look at them; if not, picture the last crowd you were in, a store, a train, a school pickup line.
Let your eyes rest on one face, then another, without judging clothes or moods, and think what Merton thought: this one is shining too. If you pray, you can bless them without words.

wordCard.voice: Transfiguration, the Gospel scene where Jesus's face shone like the sun, which Merton saw echoed in every face on a Louisville street corner. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: they will shine out, from Matthew 13:43, the just shine as the sun.
